html:
Behavioral capabilities

By ∼\sim3-6 months, infants shift from mostly sampling to actively probing the world: the representational repertoire becomes both richer and more structured as infants begin to encode stable, cross-situational regularities that support category, object, and social representations.

Stereopsis (binocular disparity; 3D vision) effectively "switches on" around ∼\sim3-4 months 1, 2, 3 and, together with rapidly improving smooth pursuit 4, increases access to metric depth and improves foreground–background parsing; stereoacuity then sharpens quickly over the following weeks 5. Depth is not just static: during 3-6 months infants increasingly maintain dynamically completed object trajectories when a moving object is temporarily hidden. By ∼\sim4 months, infants use spatiotemporal continuity constraints to anticipate where and when an occluded object should reappear (sensitive to occlusion duration), rather than treating disappearance as termination 6, 7. Even in the absence of continuous motion, infants demonstrate generative prediction over learned event structure: by ∼\sim3.5 months, infants viewing a basic spatial-temporal sequence (e.g., stimuli alternating between left and right locations) generate anticipatory saccades to the correct location before stimulus onset, including for asymmetric temporal patterns–providing a direct oculomotor readout of a predictive world model that encodes where and approximately when the next event will occur 8.

These predictions begin to couple to control: infants move from reactive tracking toward predictive pursuit and predictive reaching for moving targets, extrapolating future position to compensate for sensorimotor delays 9, 10. In a closely related vein, prediction begins to cover not only translation but also latent transformations: across this window infants can track invisible spatial transformations (e.g., an object rotating or changing orientation behind an occluder) and anticipate the post-occlusion configuration, consistent with early mental rotation / transformation-completion rather than mere reappearance timing 11, 12. Strikingly, self-generated object exploration can causally facilitate this capacity (more varied object manipulation →\rightarrow better mental-rotation performance), linking action to the acquisition of viewpoint- and transformation-invariant world models 13.

Basic-level categories emerge: early in this window, infants form category representations that generalize across novel exemplars (e.g., cats, dogs, chairs, couches) 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20. Categorization is not limited to object kinds: early in this window, infants also form basic spatial relational categories, discriminating above from below configurations of a target relative to a reference object and generalizing across changes in the identity and position of both items 21. A longitudinal study tests infants’ visual statistical learning (Figure) 107. The study compares an EEG learning index across visits (Figure).

Object representations acquire several foundational priors during this window. Early in this window, infants can perceptually complete partly occluded objects (treating disjoint visible fragments as one persisting entity) and use spatiotemporal continuity to individuate objects across disappearances–a precursor to "object files" that support stable reference 22, 23. The ’physics engine’ also updates to enforce solidity constraints: by 3.5-4.5 months, infants look significantly longer (dishabituate) when a rotating screen appears to pass through a solid block, suggesting they model objects as substantial entities that cannot occupy the same space 24. Shortly after (approx. 4.5 months), they begin to factor variable height into these occlusion models, detecting violations when a tall object disappears behind a short occluder, implying a metric calibration of the hidden world 25 By ∼\sim4.5 months, they can also use featural differences (e.g., shape/size) to decide whether an occlusion event implies one object or two, strengthening identity tracking beyond pure motion cues 26, 27. Correspondingly, physical expectations expand beyond mere tracking: infants respect simple support constraints by ∼\sim4.5 months 28 and, toward the end of this window, show increasingly explicit sensitivity to gravity-consistent dynamics, treating violations of gravity-appropriate acceleration as surprising 29. Importantly, physical expectations are acquired in an event-type-specific manner: infants use a variable like object height to detect violations during occlusion events (e.g., a tall object behind a short occluder) several months before they apply the same variable to containment events (e.g., a tall object lowered into a short container). This "decalage" implies that the infantile physics engine maintains distinct event schemas–occlusion, containment, covering–each independently calibrated through experience, rather than a single general solidity principle 30, 31.

Causal structure also becomes perceptible as an invariant over kinematics: infants discriminate causal launching from superficially similar noncausal motion (e.g., delayed reaction), implying that the world model is learning event grammars 32, 33. In parallel, the model begins sharpening agent/object priors: infants treat humans as solid, persisting entities in occlusion events (i.e., not exempt from material constraints) 34. Self-propulsion acts as a powerful cue that supports inferences not licensed for inert objects, consistent with early domain-specific expectations about agent-like motion (a precursor to explicit theory-of-mind) 35. Beyond rigid-body constraints, the physical world model also begins to differentiate ontological kinds: by ∼\sim5 months infants use motion cues to distinguish solids vs. liquids and apply different expectations about whether contents will pour vs. tumble, and whether objects will pass through vs. remain on top of a nonsolid substance–extending intuitive physics beyond "blocks and balls" 36.

The action-coupled side of these transitions is scaffolded by a posture-to-reach cascade (rolling, stable midline control, supported sitting) that reorganizes the workspace so reaching becomes reliable and multimodal object exploration becomes more systematic 37, 38. Correspondingly, object interaction becomes increasingly epistemic (chosen to reveal information): infants begin to vary exploratory actions (mouthing, rubbing, banging, rotating) as a function of object and surface properties, effectively probing affordances and learning object-action-outcome maps 39, 40. Rudimentary preshaping (anticipatory hand shaping for grasping) appears 41, 42, and raking grasps (all fingers at the same time) emerge by  6 months 43. More generally, the hands become a uniquely available near-field effector/object: sustained hand regard (watching their own hand movements) emerges during this window, providing dense closed-loop visuomotor experience with a controllable target before canonical reaching is reliable 44, 45.

Attention control improves as "sticky fixation" eases and saccadic latencies drop 46; and a minimal visual working memory ( 1 item) is measurable by  5 months 47, 48, which allows looking and reaching to be more strategic than reactive. Similarly, memory for structured action sequences becomes measurable: by ∼\sim6 months, infants can reproduce multi-step action sequences in delayed imitation paradigms (with performance depending on delay and retrieval support), indicating emerging capacity to store and reinstate ordered event models rather than only static percepts 49, 50, 51.

In language, representations begin to align with native statistics: by  4.5 months infants recognize the sound pattern of their own name 52, and by  6 months they can segment word-like units when prosodic edges or distributional cues are favorable 53; in parallel, vowel categories show the first signs of perceptual narrowing toward the native phonology 54. Familiar tokens (especially the infant’s name) act as anchors for speech segmentation 55, accelerating early lexical learning 56. In parallel, vocal control becomes more interaction-ready: infants participate in increasingly structured vocal turn-taking across this window, and the approach to ∼\sim6 months marks the onset of more syllable-like babbling (e.g "ba-ba" or "ma-ma") in typical development, providing a higher-bandwidth action channel for shaping caregiver responses 57, 58, 59, 60.

On the social side, 4-6-month-olds detect and remember specific face-voice pairings and can match facial and vocal affect, making person-specific, multimodal identity a learnable unit rather than parallel streams 61, 62. Towards the end of this window, infants are also able to discriminate expressions of happiness, sadness, and anger from visual or vocal cues alone, passing through stages where less and less temporal synchrony of multimodal cues (i.e face and voice) is required 63. Social selectivity also sharpens as face-space begins to narrow toward frequently seen categories 64, 65, changing who is tracked and imitated, while action understanding begins taking a step beyond kinematics: by  5-6 months infants may even encode the goal object of others’ reaches 66. Beyond identifying what an agent acts on, infants also evaluate how goals are pursued: by ∼\sim6 months, infants expect agents to minimize the cost of their actions (e.g., taking a shorter path when no obstacle is present), and look longer when an agent takes an unnecessarily circuitous route to a goal–even for unfamiliar, non-human agents. This efficiency principle (a nascent "teleological stance") allows the infant’s agent model to generate predictions about action trajectories from goal + context alone, going beyond kinematic pattern matching 67, 68.

Social learning also becomes increasingly triadic: by ∼\sim4.5-6 months infants can follow others’ gaze to external targets, with this behavior being shaped by perceptual cues (motion of the head) as well as social cues (gaze direction) 69, 70 and combining with an emerging ability to follow others’ pointing 71. Moreover, gaze following is selectively engaged by ostensive/communicative signals (e.g when preceded by direct gaze or infant-directed speech), implying that infants are learning when another’s attention shift is referential rather than mere motion 72. Triadic communication allows basic "social referencing" (using caregivers as emotional referents in ambiguous situations) by 6 months 73, 74, following the arc of infants’ abilities to discriminate emotions 63, but potentially remaining limited to stimuli that have both facial and vocal emotional information available for referencing 75. Also following the arc of emotion discrimination, infants begin evaluating how agents treat other agents: by 6 months, infants prefer an individual who helps another achieve a goal over one who hinders it, prefer a helper over a neutral individual, and prefer a neutral individual over a hinderer. This indicates that the world model assigns social-evaluative valence to observed agent-agent interactions on the basis of behavior toward third parties–a capacity that may serve as a biological foundation for moral cognition 76. A longitudinal study observes infant vocalizations during play (Figure) 105. The researchers measure vocal responses to caregivers (Figure). The study also measures bids at each assessment (Figure) 108. A study tracks the emergence of joint-attention bids (Figure).

Finally, abstract magnitude codes come online: six-month-olds discriminate numerosities (regardless of modality) at  1:2 ratios (e.g., 8 vs. 16 but not 8 vs. 12), indicating an approximate number system with coarse, ratio-dependent precision that can scaffold later symbolic learning 77, 78. Moreover, the approximate number system supports not just static discrimination but transformation-level predictions: by ∼\sim5 months, infants look longer at arithmetically impossible outcomes (e.g., one object is placed on stage, a screen occludes it, a second object is added behind the screen, yet only one object is revealed when the screen drops) than at the correct outcome, and analogous results hold for subtraction (2−-1). This implies that the world model tracks numerical change across occlusion and generates expectations about resultant quantities—an early form of event-based arithmetic prediction 79. Predictions also may begin to represent uncertainty rather than only deterministic regularities: by ∼\sim6 months infants may form probabilistic expectations from visible population statistics, looking longer at samples that are improbable given proportions–an early signature of "intuitive statistics" / likelihood-sensitive prediction error 80.

Training data and optimization

Training data

Tactile!

At this stage, training data becomes self-generated, closed-loop, and reweighted by posture and pedagogy. As stereopsis and smooth pursuit come online, rolling and early sitting expand the workspace and create rich self-motion (optic flow, motion parallax, head-hand reafference), with each curiosity-driven reach yielding a tightly time-locked packet of retinal slip, proprioception, sound, and haptics that the system can align and learn from.

Manual exploration multiplies contingencies: by  5-6 months infants vary mouthing, scratching, shaking, and banging with size, texture, mass, and sound, producing multimodal contingencies that inform proto physics-and-objects models.

Concurrently, a vocal-auditory loop spins up: coos, squeals, and marginal babble generate controllable acoustic features that are rife with cheap prediction errors; caregivers mirror, praise, and time turn-taking, converting phonation control into supervised data. A study records infant movement and vocalization together (Figure) 106. The study compares movement around vocalization onset (Figure).

Caregivers further shape the input distribution: infant-directed speech and "motionese" (slower, exaggerated actions), name cues, contingent touch, direct gaze, and structured routines (peekaboo, turn-taking) function as high-SNR micro-curricula and increase temporal alignment across modalities; affective touch and cardiorespiratory rhythms supply slow interoceptive/affective structure that gates precision and learning rate.

Sticky mittens evidence

Causally, experimentally boosting early prehension via the "sticky mittens" paradigm (Velcro mittens that let pre-reaching ∼\sim3-month-olds lift objects through contact) has been shown to increase object-directed engagement and manual exploration (e.g., more sustained contact/manipulation and more coordinated looking–acting patterns) relative to matched observational/passive experience, with some reports of downstream carryover; however, recent critical and preregistered work suggests the size/robustness of motor gains can be context-dependent 81, 82, 83, 84, 85.

pre-reaching 3-month-olds given brief "sticky mittens" experience (Velcro-enabled grasping) subsequently encode the goal object of another person’s reach in violation-of-expectation tasks, whereas age-matched infants without this experience do not—demonstrating that first-person motor competence causally scaffolds the agent model’s capacity to represent others’ action goals 86. The preregistered study reports reaching outcomes (Figure) 104. A preregistered study compares sticky-mitten and control experiences (Figure).

Optimization

These rich, time-locked, cross-modal data streams (disparity + pursuit + contact; face-voice; shake->sound) saturate the underlying optimizers, shifting the system’s objective from generic calibration toward controllability and precise perception.

Cerebellar microcomplexes run supervised calibration on eyes and arms: each visually guided reach or pursuit episode yields direction- and timing-specific climbing-fiber teaching signals that retune Purkinje output and update forward models; optic flow and fingertip contact provide high-SNR labels.

Basal-ganglia actor-critic loops exploit distributional dopamine codes to update policies from sparse successes ("act->auditory/visual consequence"), while tonic dopamine tracks opportunity cost and scales vigor so controllable, information-rich actions are repeated, consolidated, and pursued; eligibility traces ensure the right corticostriatal synapses get credited.

Cortical predictive coding becomes cheaper and more specific because error units now receive targeted, tightly synchronized, cross-modal mismatches (mouth motion->expected phoneme; hand motion->expected sound/feel), so local updates discover better representations with fewer samples; acetylcholine up-weights sensory-error precision during focused bouts, noradrenaline raises learning rates or resets policy under volatility, and serotonin lengthens the temporal horizon and lowers subjective effort as manipulation bouts extend. Transthalamic controllers (pulvinar/MD, gated by TRN) set large-scale precision and synchrony for feedback, opening apical dendritic write windows when engagement/attention is high (e.g., ostentive/demonstrative gaze).

Overnight, sleep compiles the day’s dataset: growing spindle density and tighter slow-oscillation coupling support abstraction, generalization, and pruning, with replay favoring recent, salient, or socially-tagged episodes.

retention of these event models depends on timely sleep consolidation: 6-month-olds who nap within ∼\sim4 hours of encoding successfully reproduce the target action sequence 24 hours later, whereas those who remain awake during this window do not, even when total wake time is equated—implying that offline replay during sleep is already integral to stabilizing event-level representations 87.

Net objective weights reallocate accordingly: speech moves from generic acoustic compression toward fidelity for native contrasts (helped by name-anchored segmentation), exploration prioritizes information gain about controllable object properties (size, texture, mass, sound), and social pedagogy increases the value of people-contingent outcomes.

Neural development

During this stage, the optimizers scale up: oscillations organize, conduction speeds up, networks segregate, and white matter lays down more of the bandwidth that later supports long-range inference. In scalp EEG, a posterior dominant rhythm emerges around  3 months (not the adult 10 Hz but a 3-5 Hz occipital rhythm that gradually accelerates 88) alongside a progressive flattening of the aperiodic 1/f slope 89, both pointing to maturing E/I balance and shorter effective synaptic time constants that support faster, more precisely timed plasticity.

Sleep architecture also shifts: classic N2 spindles, which first appear by  6-8 weeks, lengthen and strengthen through month 4-5, while REM proportion drops toward  30% by  6 months–changes that increase offline signal-to-noise as more room is made for replay and thalamo-cortical consolidation 90, 91.

Structurally, white-matter bandwidth rises rapidly and heterogenously: quantitative MRI shows longitudinal relaxation rate (R1) (a myelin-linked measure) increasing from birth to 6 months across all bundles with faster gains in initially immature segments and along inferior->superior and posterior->anterior gradients (a well-documented progression of myelination that plays out across decades development); myelin-water and T1w/T2w maps replicate the early occipital->parietal->callosal gradient across 3-11 months 92, 93. As a convergent, non-MRI readout of conduction speed, visual cortical responses shorten sharply: infant visual N1/P1 latencies drop nonlinearly with rapid change through  6-9 months, consistent with faster afferent and intracortical transmission 94. This recent study illustrates fig. 2 (Figure). This recent study illustrates fig. 3 (Figure).

At the network level, the connectome shifts from mostly local coupling to more segregated-yet-cohering large-scale systems 95: thalamocortical connectivity differentiates along sensory-specific motifs and strengthens its overall integration with cortex 96; within-network synchrony rises in primary sensorimotor, auditory, and visual systems 97 (although some is present from birth 98). The global sensorimotor network splits into mouth and hand submodules by  6 months 99, the dorsal attention network becomes detectable around 6 months 99, and default-mode components appear as anterior and posterior nodes that remain relatively segregated rather than an integrated midline core 97. The salience and fronto-parietal networks remain largely unsynchronized at this stage 97.

Synaptically, V1 is in its exuberant growth phase: classic histology places the most rapid synapse production around  2-4 months, with high density through  8-12 months before prolonged pruning; this transient overparameterization increases representational capacity and sample efficiency before compression 100, 101, 102, a common motif across brain regions which tracks behavioral development (e.g the PFC is the last region to reach full exuberance and then to be fully pruned, taking multiple decades).

Key learning gates are open: the sensitive/critical period (sensitive = strong bias in plasticity (best time to learn, but not the only time); critical = hard cutoff (learning must occur within window, or it’s lost forever)) for binocular alignment and stereopsis is most vulnerable around  3-4 months (with susceptibility extending into later childhood) 2, and the first phonetic reorganization toward native speech begins by  6 months 103, together shaping the priors for depth and language that downstream circuits will build on.

The 3-6-month gains are only possible because 0-3 months pre-trained the whole stack: early sensory codes were already being carved by prediction errors as contrast sensitivity climbed  2.4->4.0 cyc/deg from 1->3 months, motion selectivity appeared by  5 weeks, and face-selective N290/P400 components emerged by  3 months-so by this window, ventral/dorsal representations are not learning from scratch but refining an initialized basis. Offline, REM twitches and the first N2 spindles had already supplied labeled sensorimotor tuples and consolidation windows during  14-17 h/day of sleep, seeding calibrated somatosensory/motor maps that 3-6-month cerebello-cortical loops now exploit for faster forward-model updates. On the control side, the system entered this stage with a working operant channel: by 2-3 months infants showed acquisition->extinction->retention in the mobile-conjugate paradigm, evidence that cortico-basal-ganglia actor-critic machinery had already begun assigning credit to actions, which 3-6-month exploration then scales up into richer policies. The sampling policy itself was bootstrapped by caregivers and social rewards during the "two-month shift": mutual gaze and the social smile turned interactions into high-SNR, quasi-labeled episodes that continue to gate what is learned next in the 3-6-month window (e.g., person-specific face-voice bindings and joint-attention precursors). The systems handoff described for 0-3 months (moving from transient, endogenously dominated regimes to thalamo-cortically gated, externally driven processing) means that by 3-6 months rising oscillatory structure and conduction speed can actually be used: predictive loops run with better signal-to-noise, long-range coupling starts to stabilize, and visuomotor controllers shift from reflex reduction (e.g., OKN asymmetry) toward predictive pursuit.
